source: Hong and Page (2004) Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers (numbers as reported by Reijula and Kuorikoski 2021)
finding: Founding ringworld simulation. Agents search a circular landscape with jump heuristics. A random group beat a group of the best individual agents.
numbers: Parameters l=12, k=3, n=2000 positions, payoffs uniform 0-100. Best individual agents scored 87.3, worst 84.3. Groups of 10: high-ability group 92.56, random group 94.53.
limits: Full PNAS text was blocked (reCAPTCHA / 403); numbers taken from the secondary source that replicated them.
agent_relevance: The classic claim is a mechanism for diverse attempts, but the effect is only 2 points on a 100 scale and the proof is about possibility, not size.

source: Reijula and Kuorikoski (2021) The diversity-ability trade-off in scientific problem solving
finding: Replicated the ringworld result, then showed it is fragile. In the original bit-string model of Hong and Page (2001) there was no systematic diversity advantage at all.
numbers: Ringworld replication reproduced the 92.56 vs 94.53 style gap. Gap correlated .65 with the difference in effective group size (overlap-free heuristic size). In nearly half of random groups the group heuristic was the full set [1..12]; only 13% of random groups had effective size below 11.
limits: Simulation only. Authors built their own stairway model, so it is built to reward ability too.
agent_relevance: Diversity wins mostly because high-ability members are redundant, so the group is effectively smaller. For our agent: copies of one strong model are the extreme case of redundancy.
quote: the model employs an impoverished implementation of the problem-solving task

source: Reijula and Kuorikoski (2021) stairway landscape result
finding: On landscapes where ability matters (a hidden increasing sequence needing specific jumps), high-ability groups win for small groups and simple problems. Diversity wins only when the problem needs more heuristics than any one agent holds.
numbers: Parameters l=3, k=12, n=2000, 100 repetitions over 100 landscapes (50x50 for the difficulty sweep). Above group size 10 the random group catches up and no significant gap remains. Ability dominates at small group size and small step set; random groups get a slight edge at large group size and large step set.
limits: Toy model; authors admit it is built to favour ability. Effect sizes shown as colour maps, not tabulated.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: diversity pays when a task is complex enough that one solver cannot hold all needed skills. For a single model with one skill set that is rarely the case, so best-model plus many samples is the safer default (G4).

source: Reijula and Kuorikoski (2021) critique of landscape randomness
finding: Hong-Page landscapes are pure noise, so heuristics have nothing to exploit and ability barely differs between agents. Smoothing the landscape (Grim et al. 2019) still gives only minute differences.
numbers: Best vs worst individual agent differ by 3.0 points (87.3 vs 84.3) on a 0-100 scale.
limits: Argument from simulation parameters, not from new human data.
agent_relevance: Do not cite the 2004 result as evidence that weaker or different agents beat strong ones on structured tasks.

source: Grim, Singer, Bramson et al. (2019) Diversity, ability, and expertise in epistemic communities
finding: Extended the Hong-Page model to landscapes of different randomness and showed the diversity-trumps-ability result is sensitive to landscape structure.
numbers: Abstract only: no figures read. Reijula and Kuorikoski state Grim et al. reproduced the 2004 results and that smoothing gave only small differences.
limits: Abstract and secondary description only; full text not opened.
agent_relevance: Advice from the authors: do not read such models too broadly. Diversity benefit depends on task terrain.

source: Thompson (2014) Does diversity trump ability? An example of the misuse of mathematics
finding: Mathematical critique of the Hong-Page theorem: after technical corrections it is a statement of possibility. The group wins because it is random, not because it is diverse.
numbers: No numbers read. Described in Singer 2019 abstract and Reijula and Kuorikoski.
limits: AMS Notices page blocked by bot check; not opened.
agent_relevance: The theorem gives no guarantee that a diverse group beats experts in a given task.

source: Singer (2019) Diversity, not randomness, trumps ability
finding: Defends the diversity reading against Thompson. Says we should be clearer about how functional diversity is conceived and measured.
numbers: No numbers (abstract only).
limits: Abstract via Crossref only.
agent_relevance: Key design point: measure diversity as difference in what solvers do (heuristic overlap), not as random assignment.

source: Luan, Katsikopoulos and Reimer (2012) When does diversity trump ability in group decision making? A simulation study
finding: Three simulations with take-the-best (accurate, homogeneous) vs minimalist (less accurate, diverse) groups. Every manipulation that cut individual accuracy also raised diversity, so the two conflicted.
numbers: Group size 1 to 100 in Study 1. A minimalist group of 100 still lagged far behind a take-the-best group when cues differed greatly in validity. Group accuracy peaked at an intermediate error level in the cue information.
limits: Cue-based binary decision task, simulated agents.
agent_relevance: Rule: ability matters more when option quality differs greatly; diversity matters more when quality differences are small. Check how uneven the quality of our candidate strategies is before diversifying.
quote: individual accuracy is more important in task environments in which cues differ greatly in the quality of their information

source: Alexander, Himmelreich and Thompson (2015) Epistemic landscapes, optimal search, and the division of cognitive labor
finding: Re-analysis of Weisberg and Muldoon (2009): their finding that novelty-seeking 'maverick' search beats following others was due to modelling errors. They also say social learning may not help in epistemically complex landscapes.
numbers: No numbers (abstract only).
limits: Abstract only; the full text not opened.
agent_relevance: Failed-replication class: the landscape model result that mavericks help does not survive correction. Do not build 'novelty-seeking attempt' operators on it.

source: Weisberg and Muldoon (2009) Epistemic landscapes and the division of cognitive labor
finding: Agent-based model of scientists on a hill landscape with three strategies: independent, follower, maverick (avoid explored ground). Reported benefits of a mixed population.
numbers: No numbers read (abstract only).
limits: Contested by Alexander et al. 2015; abstract only.
agent_relevance: Source of the 'diversity of attempts' idea for scaffolds, but weak support.

source: Authors not confirmed (2025) When Diversity in Voting Trumps Ability, Episteme
finding: Gives the diversity-trumps-ability idea a rigorous form inside an approval-voting Condorcet jury model. Diversity means low correlation with an opinion leader; ability means competence margin.
numbers: Theorem 2 bound valid for pi < dp/(dp+1). Example: m=20, dp=0.4, p_hat=0.8, n=100, pi=0.1 gives P_min=0.85. Diverse group wins when epsilon >= (lambda - pi*lambda)/(dp+1); with n=100, m=5, dp=0.5, pi=0.2, lambda=0.1 the threshold is about 0.053.
limits: Read through a fetched summary of the Cambridge page; author names were not shown. Voting model, not search.
agent_relevance: Gives an explicit trade-off: a small drop in error correlation can offset a larger drop in competence. This is the cleanest formal link to G4 (correlated samples).

source: Horwitz and Horwitz (2007) The effects of team diversity on team outcomes: a meta-analytic review of team demography
finding: Human teams. Task-related diversity (skills, function) is positively related to team performance. Bio-demographic diversity is not significantly related.
numbers: Abstract gives direction only; effect sizes not read.
limits: Abstract only. Field studies, mixed settings.
agent_relevance: Support for diversity of task-relevant knowledge, not diversity as such.

source: Bell, Villado, Lukasik et al. (2011) Getting specific about demographic diversity variable and team performance relationships
finding: Meta-analysis split diversity into specific variables (functional background, tenure and so on) rather than broad categories.
numbers: No effect sizes read.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Supports measuring diversity per dimension. Which dimension matters for a model is unknown.

source: Li, Lin, Xia and Jin (2025) Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents: is mixing different LLMs beneficial?
finding: Self-MoA (many samples from the single best model) beat mixing different models in most settings.
numbers: AlpacaEval 2.0 LC win rate: mixed MoA 59.1 vs Self-MoA 65.7 (+6.6). Average +3.8 across MMLU-redux, CRUX, MATH. Self-MoA on gemma-2-9b-it-WPO-HB reached 78.5 (new top at the time).
limits: Single-model gains depend on picking the strongest proposer, which needs a prior measurement of quality.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G4: for one strong model, repeated sampling beats importing weaker models.

source: Li et al. (2025) Rethinking MoA: quality-diversity regression
finding: Over 200 mixtures, MoA accuracy rises with both quality and diversity, but is far more sensitive to quality. Best results sit at high quality and low diversity.
numbers: Linear regression of MoA score on quality and diversity (Vendi score), about 70 points per dataset: R2 = 0.771, 0.685, 0.760 across the three datasets, both coefficients p<0.001.
limits: Diversity measured with the Vendi score on outputs; a proxy.
agent_relevance: Quality-diversity trade-off in LLMs matches the ability side of Hong-Page. Rank candidate strategies by quality first.

source: Li et al. (2025) Rethinking MoA: when mixing helps
finding: Mixing different models helps only when models have complementary specialities. In a task built so each model excels at one subtask, only two of 13 Mixed-MoA settings slightly beat Self-MoA.
numbers: Specialised proposers (Qwen2-7B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite, Qwen2-Math-7B). On the specialised-model benchmarks the task-best single-model Self-MoA beat all 13 Mixed-MoA settings across tasks; in a constructed mixture task, Mixed-MoA beat Self-MoA of dddddd.
limits: Small 7B-class proposers; may not transfer to frontier models.
agent_relevance: Matches the stairway result: diversity pays when no single solver holds all needed skills.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Mixture-of-Agents enhances LLM capabilities
finding: Layered MoA of open models reached 65.1% on AlpacaEval 2.0 vs 57.5% for GPT-4o. Using different LLMs as proposers beat the same LLM sampled repeatedly.
numbers: Table 3: n=6 proposers: multiple-proposer 61.3% vs single-proposer 56.7%; n=3: 58.0 vs 56.1; n=2: 58.8 vs 54.5; n=1: 47.8 both. Qwen1.5-110B aggregator, 2 layers.
limits: Their single-proposer choice was a weaker model; Li et al. found the opposite when the strongest model is the proposer.
agent_relevance: The mixed result: cross-model diversity beats same-weak-model sampling, but loses to same-strongest-model sampling.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng and Garg (2025) Correlated errors in large language models
finding: LLM errors are strongly correlated across models. Larger and more accurate models are more correlated, even across providers.
numbers: 349 LLMs on 12,032 questions (HuggingFace), 71 on 14,042 (HELM), 20 on 1,800 resume pairs. On HELM, models agree about 60% when both are wrong (random 1/3). Mean error agreement 0.423 on HuggingFace; random baseline 0.127; 97.5% to 100% of pairs above baseline. Features explain 34-62% of variance in agreement. One pair agrees on 0.9987 of questions both get wrong.
limits: Multiple-choice benchmarks and one hiring task.
agent_relevance: Cross-model diversity gives less independence than assumed, and the best models are least independent. Supports G4: agreement is a hint only.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Correlated errors: downstream effect in LLM-as-judge
finding: A judge model inflates the accuracy of models weaker than itself because they share wrong answers.
numbers: Reported as a systematic inflation pattern; exact values per judge in the paper's figure.
limits: Exact percentages not copied.
agent_relevance: Do not let one model judge the output of a similar model as proof of correctness.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: open-ended homogeneity of language models
finding: Within-model repetition and across-model homogeneity on 26K open-ended queries (Infinity-Chat) across 42 models.
numbers: With top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0 average pairwise similarity among responses to one prompt typically exceeds 0.8. Cross-model similarity ranges 71% to 82% (DeepSeek-V3 and qwen-max 0.82). With min-p 0.1, temperature 2.0 similarity still exceeds 0.8 on average; with min-p, 81% of pairs exceed 0.7 and 61.2% exceed 0.8. Paraphrased prompts: within-prompt 0.821, cross-paraphrase 0.781.
limits: Open-ended generation, embedding similarity as the measure.
agent_relevance: Sampling temperature and model swaps give little real diversity. Diversity must come from structure (different strategies, tools, evidence) rather than noise.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) When a helpful assistant is not really helpful: personas in system prompts
finding: Adding 162 personas to system prompts did not improve MMLU accuracy over no persona across 4 model families.
numbers: 162 roles, 2,410 MMLU questions, 4 model families. Choosing the best persona per question and aggregating helped, but automatic persona selection was no better than random.
limits: Factual multiple choice; effects of persona on open tasks differ.
agent_relevance: Supports G4 text: no persona voters on single-answer problems. Persona diversity is not real cognitive diversity.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? multi-agent debate strategies
finding: Multi-agent debate does not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling over multiple reasoning paths. After tuning, Multi-Persona improves.
numbers: Medprompt best overall; e.g. MedQA 0.65, PubMedQA 0.77, MMLU 0.74, CosmosQA 0.48 for Medprompt. Adjusting agent agreement level improved debate.
limits: Mostly GPT-3.5 and GPT-4; sensitive to hyperparameters.
agent_relevance: Interaction among same-model agents adds cost; independent sampling plus a vote is a strong baseline.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving factuality and reasoning through multiagent debate
finding: Three ChatGPT agents with two debate rounds beat single answers, reflection and majority vote.
numbers: Arithmetic: single 67.0, reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8. GSM8K: 77.0, 75.0, 81.0, 85.0. Chess move quality 91.4, 102.1, 102.2, 122.9.
limits: Later work (Choi 2025, Smit 2024, Zhang 2025) found much of this gain comes from voting, not debate.
agent_relevance: Original positive case, now contested. Also shows ChatGPT and Bard debate fixed an error in one example.

source: Choi, Zhu and Li (2025) Debate or Vote: which yields better decisions in multi-agent LLMs?
finding: Across 7 benchmarks, majority voting alone accounts for most of the gain attributed to multi-agent debate. Theory: debate induces a martingale over beliefs, so expected correctness does not change.
numbers: Mean agent accuracy trajectories over debate rounds are essentially flat (Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B). Targeted interventions that bias updates toward correction do help.
limits: Theory assumes homogeneous, fully connected agents; the heterogeneous case is argued separately.
agent_relevance: Independent attempts plus an aggregation rule capture most of the value. Debate needs a correction signal.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop overvaluing multi-agent debate; embrace model heterogeneity
finding: 5 MAD methods across 9 benchmarks and 4 models often failed to beat chain-of-thought and self-consistency. Mixing two models (Heter-MAD) improved every MAD framework.
numbers: Heter-MAD (GPT-4o-mini and Llama3.1-70b, p=0.5): SoM +6.4% vs SoM average, +5.8% vs CoT average; EoT +8.2%; ChatEval +4.0%; AgentVerse +2.7%. Average accuracy 76.7 vs 69.9 to 74.3 for single-model SoM. Some benchmarks negative vs CoT (for example MBPP -2.0% to -10.8%).
limits: Two models of similar strength; gains are modest and not uniform.
agent_relevance: Conflicts with Li et al. only if the two models are of unequal strength: heterogeneity helps when strengths are comparable.

source: Chen, Saha and Bansal (2024) ReConcile: round-table conference among diverse LLMs
finding: Diverse model agents discussing and voting by confidence beat single-model debate. Removing the multi-model component cost the most accuracy.
numbers: StrategyQA: ReConcile 79.0 vs 72.2 with three ChatGPT instances (about 6.8 points); without grouping 76.7; without convincingness 74.5; without confidence 77.7. ANLI: 57.7 vs best debate 48.3 (9.4 points over debate). Up to 11.4% over baselines.
limits: Uses ChatGPT, Bard and Claude2; diversity measured with BERTScore (multi-model responses least similar).
agent_relevance: Direct LLM evidence for the diversity effect when the models are of similar level.

source: Naik et al. (2024) Diversity of thought improves reasoning abilities of LLMs (DIV-SE)
finding: Ensembling across diverse approach prompts from one model beat self-consistency at the same or lower cost.
numbers: GPT-4 zero-shot CoT: Graph Coloring CoT 15.0, SC-10 23.0, IDIV-SE 74.0, DIV-SE 97.0; Blocksworld 3: 70, 73, 82, 94; Blocksworld 4/5: 40.0, 41.2, 57.0, 69.6. MATH GPT-4: DIV-SE +14.3 (few-shot) and +16.87 points (zero-shot) over baseline.
limits: Prompt diversity generated by the same model; some of the gain is from stronger approach prompts, not diversity alone.
agent_relevance: Structural diversity inside one model (different approaches) works where sampling noise does not. Fits the plan: diversity of attempts via approach, with G4 limits on voting.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large language monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Coverage (any sample correct) rises log-linearly with samples, but picking the right one needs a verifier; majority voting and reward models plateau.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 (prior single-sample SOTA 43%). MATH with Llama-3-8B: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000; majority voting or reward model only 40.50% to 41.41%.
limits: Coverage needs a verifier to be useful; in math word problems verification is weak.
agent_relevance: Many attempts help only if a check can find the correct one. Pair diversity with verification (G-rules on checks).

source: Li et al. (2024) More agents is all you need (Agent Forest)
finding: Sampling and voting over many instances of the same model scales performance with number of agents; the gain grows with task difficulty.
numbers: No single headline number copied in this session.
limits: Gains reported as orthogonal to other methods; exact figures not read.
agent_relevance: Supports same-model sampling plus vote as a baseline that other methods must beat.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail? (MAST)
finding: Taxonomy of 14 failure modes in 3 groups: system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification, from 150 annotated traces.
numbers: Failure rates 41% to 86.7% across 7 open-source multi-agent systems; inter-annotator kappa 0.88.
limits: Open-source MAS frameworks only.
agent_relevance: Multi-agent diversity has its own failure costs; verification gaps are a main cause.
